Who sends and collects the property tax bill in Albany, NY?

The City of Albany Treasurer collects the bill, and the City Assessor sets the value it is based on. The Treasurer's office is in City Hall at 24 Eagle Street, and the phone number is 518-434-5036. The Assessor's office is on the third floor of the same building in Room 302, reachable at 518-434-5155.

Albany sits on the west bank of the Hudson River, about ten miles south of where the Mohawk River joins it, and has been New York's capital since 1797. The city is also the seat of Albany County, and its housing ranges from row houses near the river to newer streets around Buckingham Pond. Under the City Charter the Treasurer is the chief fiscal officer and handles collection of all city taxes and money owed to the city.

  • Treasurer: tax bills, payments, receipts, address changes, returned payments.
  • Assessor: assessed values, STAR and other exemption applications, grievance forms, parcel maps.
  • Board of Assessment Review: hears assessment complaints. The Common Council appoints its members to five-year terms.

When are Albany property taxes due, and what happens if I pay late?

The full bill, or the first half if you split it, is due by January 31. Eligible seniors get until February 6. When January 31 lands on a weekend, the deadline moves to the next business day, and in 2027 that falls on a Sunday, so the practical date is Monday, February 1.

Albany now lets every owner pay in two installments. The first installment is half the bill. The second half is billed in early July and can be paid any time after the first installment, with interest added. Installments must be paid by check or cash, because the online system takes full payments only.

Bills should reach your mailbox by January 12. If yours has not come by then, print it from the Treasurer's online lookup instead of calling. The city states that state law requires penalties on late payments in every case, and the municipality cannot waive the interest. A returned payment costs $34.

What is the waste collection fee on an Albany tax bill?

It is a separate charge of $180 per unit that appears on the property tax bill itself. Before 2026 the city mailed that fee as its own bill. Unpaid amounts from the prior year, listed as $90 per unit for 2025, are carried onto the 2026 tax bill along with added late charges.

Owners who believe the fee should not apply to them can email the Treasurer or call 518-434-5036 to request an exemption application. The city notes that it did not place the fee on 2025 bills for owners it already knew to be exempt in 2023 and 2024.

This matters when you sell. A previous year's fee that went unpaid becomes part of the tax bill, so it belongs in the payoff total. Ask the Treasurer for a figure that includes it, and check the total against the bill you received in January.

How do I pay my Albany property tax?

You can pay by mail, online, or in person at City Hall. The office recommends against bill-payment services, because their envelopes usually carry no postmark, and the city counts the date by the USPS postmark and ignores a postage meter mark.

  • By mail: make the check payable to City of Albany and send it to City Treasurer, Room 109, City Hall, Albany, NY 12207. Include the bill number, your signature and the date, plus any interest owed.
  • Online: e-check costs 50 cents. A credit card costs 25 cents plus 1.95 percent of the payment. Online payments can take up to five business days to show.
  • In person: Room 110 at City Hall, weekdays from 8:30 a.m., with later hours from January 29 to 31.

Send a self-addressed stamped envelope if you want a receipt right away. Otherwise receipts go out in bulk in late March or April, and e-receipts post online within 48 hours of a payment.

How do I challenge an Albany assessment?

File a grievance complaint with the Assessor after May 1 and no later than Grievance Day, the fourth Tuesday in May. Forms are available at the Assessor's office starting May 1. The Board of Assessment Review decides the complaint under Chapter 42 of the Albany General Code.

Assessments change in Albany because of new construction, fires, demolitions and periodic citywide updates meant to keep the roll even. You can look at any parcel on the maps kept in the Assessor's office. Bring a recent sale of a similar house nearby, a repair estimate or an appraisal, since the board decides on value and does not weigh how large the bill feels.

Which exemptions and STAR benefits apply in Albany?

Exemption applications are accepted from January 1 through March 1, filed at the Assessor's office. Basic STAR is for owners who live in the home, and every owner must sign the application and supply a photocopy of a driver's license as proof of residence. Call 518-434-5155 for help with Enhanced STAR.

The state's Tax Department now pays STAR as a credit you register for once. It issues the payment before your school tax is due and keeps paying each year while you stay eligible. Anyone who sells the home should close the registration, and the buyer registers as soon as the house is a primary residence.

What happens to unpaid Albany tax when I sell the house?

Any balance is settled from your sale proceeds at closing, and the current year is split between you and the buyer on the closing statement. You do not need to bring cash to the table, but the payoff has to be right, so ask the Treasurer for the number before the closing date. The office takes calls at 518-434-5036 on weekdays.

  • Ask the Treasurer for the current balance, including any carried-over waste collection fee, and keep the answer in an email.
  • If the first installment is paid and the July half is not yet billed, expect a proration credit to the buyer for the months you owned.
  • Confirm with the Assessor that your exemption is removed or transferred in line with the new owner's status.

A buyer who pays cash and closes quickly can settle the same payoff, so owing the city does not stop a sale. It only changes how much is left for you after the closing statement.

What does the housing market around Albany look like?

Albany is a small, dense city of about 21 square miles. Older sections near the river are mostly row houses, which often carry older roofs, porches and boilers that a buyer will inspect. The Pine Bush preserve, once about 25,000 acres, has shrunk to roughly 6,000 acres because of development on the city's western edge.

With owners in fewer than four of ten homes, many Albany sellers are landlords of small multifamily buildings. They should confirm each unit's waste collection fee before the payoff request.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Albany property tax deadline?

January 31, or February 6 for eligible seniors, with the next business day used when it falls on a weekend. In 2027 that moves the deadline to February 1. Mailed payments count by USPS postmark.

Can I split my Albany tax bill into two payments?

Yes. Pay half by the January deadline and the rest after the July bill goes out, with interest. The installment option accepts checks or cash only and is unavailable online.

Where do I get a copy of my Albany tax bill or receipt?

From the Treasurer's online lookup or by emailing the Treasurer's billing address. Receipts are mailed in bulk in late March or April, and online receipts appear within 48 hours.

When is Albany Grievance Day?

It is the fourth Tuesday in May. Forms are available from May 1 at the Assessor's office in City Hall Room 302, and the complaint must be filed by Grievance Day.

Do I owe Albany tax if I sell mid-year?

You owe the share for the months you owned the house. The closing statement splits the year, and any unpaid balance is paid to the Treasurer from your proceeds, so request the payoff figure before the closing date.

Who bills and collects property tax in Amherst, NY?

The Amherst Town Clerk's office doubles as the Receiver of Taxes and collects the Town and County bill, while the Assessor's Office sets the assessed value. Both work out of Town Hall at 5583 Main Street in Williamsville. The Town Clerk's number is 716-631-7021, and the Assessor's is 716-631-7038.

Amherst is a suburb of Buffalo in northern Erie County. The state created it in 1818 out of the town of Buffalo, and it covers 53.6 square miles that include the village of Williamsville and the hamlets of Eggertsville, Getzville, Snyder, Swormville and East Amherst. A property tax bill here has several layers, so know which office answers which question.

  • Town Clerk and Receiver of Taxes: Town and County tax bills and payments.
  • Assessor: values, exemptions, name and mailing address corrections, assessment challenges.
  • Village of Williamsville Clerk: village tax for properties inside the village, at 632-4120 (option 9).
  • Your school district: school tax dates are set separately, so ask the district.

When is Amherst Town and County tax due?

The due date is February 15. When that day lands on a weekend, the town extends it, and for 2026 the deadline was Tuesday, February 17, because February 15 was a Sunday and Town Hall was closed on the Monday holiday. The town's notice also says full and partial payments are accepted at the Town Clerk's office until June 30, with penalties added after the deadline.

The Town Clerk's office is open weekdays from 8:30 a.m. to 4 p.m. and does not close for lunch. A drop box at the back door of Town Hall is available around the clock, and a payment left there after hours and before midnight on the due date is not treated as late.

Property tax is not lump sum only. The assessor's FAQ says partial payments are accepted in any dollar amount, as many times as needed, but any balance left after the due date accrues interest and penalties on the schedule printed on the back of the bill.

How can I make sure my Amherst payment is not late?

Deliver it in a way that does not rely on a mailbox postmark. In December 2025 the postal service explained that a postmark now reflects the day mail reaches a regional processing hub, which can add one to three days after you drop it at a local post office.

  • Ask for a hand-stamped postmark at a post office counter.
  • Send it by certified or registered mail.
  • Use the Town Hall drop box at the back entrance.
  • Pay online through the town website, where you search your owner name or address in the tax bill lookup.
  • Pay in person at the Town Clerk's office.

The town discourages paying through your bank's online bill pay. Those checks arrive in bulk mail from a processing center with no postmark at all, and the town says anyone who uses that route does so at their own risk.

How do I challenge my Amherst assessment?

Start with an informal review at the Assessor's Office, then file a formal complaint on form RP-524 before Grievance Day. The next Grievance Day is Tuesday, May 25, 2027, and the town says to check back after May 1 for the hearing details.

Informal review information is posted each year after March 1. The 2026 roll used a valuation date of July 1, 2025 and a taxable status date of March 1, 2026. The Assessor offers separate review applications for residential, condominium, commercial and vacant land parcels.

The town stresses that the Assessor does not set the tax levy. Your case should rest on market value, supported by comparable sales of similar houses in your area, with attention to location, style, age and size. A five-year-old house and a fifty-year-old house are not comparable. Copies you hand in stay with the Board of Assessment Review, so keep your own set.

What does Amherst's official page say about buying or selling mid-year?

The owner on the tax due date answers for the whole bill, whether or not the bill arrived. If you bought partway through the year, you still owe the entire bill, though the closing statement normally prorates it and the seller credits you for the months before you owned the house.

The page explains that the attorney who handled the closing calculates that credit, and the seller does not send any partial payment to the tax collector. For a seller, this means the unpaid current tax should be settled from your proceeds by the closing attorney, and the number on the closing statement should match the Receiver's own figure.

If the name or mailing address on the bill is wrong, the Assessor, not the Town Clerk, corrects it. Fix that before listing so the bill does not go astray during the sale. The Assessor also answers questions about the RPTL charge on a Town and County bill, a line that can represent one-time charges rather than regular tax, so ask about it before you assume the payoff is wrong.

The numbers below describe the whole town, which includes Williamsville and the hamlets. A given street can run well above or below them. The town is also home to the north campus of the University at Buffalo and to a campus of Erie Community College, which is worth knowing if your house sits near either.

What should I check before selling an Amherst house with tax due?

Ask for the exact balance before the closing, because partial payments, penalties and any village charges can all change it. A short checklist keeps the sale on schedule.

  • Call the Town Clerk at 716-631-7021 for the Town and County balance.
  • If the property is in Williamsville, call the village clerk for the village portion.
  • Ask your school district for its balance, since it bills on its own schedule.
  • Confirm the owner name and mailing address on file with the Assessor.

A buyer paying cash can close on a short timeline, and the payoffs come out of the sale price just as in a financed sale.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Amherst property tax due date?

February 15 for Town and County tax. In 2026 it moved to Tuesday, February 17 because the 15th fell on a Sunday and Town Hall was closed Monday. Partial payments are accepted at the Town Clerk's office until June 30.

Can I pay Amherst taxes in installments?

Yes, in any dollar amount and as many payments as it takes. Any unpaid balance after the due date accrues interest and penalties, as shown on the schedule on the back of your bill.

Is there a drop box for Amherst tax payments?

Yes. It sits at the back door of Town Hall at 5583 Main Street and is open around the clock. Payments left there after hours, up to midnight on the due date, are not counted as late.

When is Amherst Grievance Day?

Tuesday, May 25, 2027. Formal complaints use form RP-524, and informal reviews are posted after March 1. The Assessor's Office at 716-631-7038 can explain both.

Who do I call about Williamsville village tax?

Who collects property tax in the Town of Brookhaven, NY?

The Town's Receiver of Taxes collects the bill from December 1 through May 31, and the Suffolk County Comptroller takes over after that. The tax office sits in Town Hall at 1 Independence Hill in Farmingville, and its phone number is 631-451-9009. The Assessor works from the same building.

Brookhaven is the second most populous town in New York, a Suffolk County town on Long Island with a 2020 Census count of 485,773 and 259.65 square miles of land. Its first English settlement, at Setauket, dates to 1655. The town reaches from Port Jefferson and Stony Brook on the North Shore to Patchogue on the South Shore, so a single tax office serves hamlets with very different school districts and home prices.

The Receiver's office says it only collects. It does not set rates. School budgets come from your school district, the county levy from the county budget, and the town levy from the Supervisor and Town Board.

What is the Brookhaven tax year, and when are bills mailed?

Town, county and school taxes in Suffolk County cover December 1 through November 30 of the following year. The bill becomes a lien on December 1, and the town mails it in mid-December. The town says you should have it by December 15. If it has not come by the third week of December, call the tax office.

The online tax system closed for the 2025 to 2026 tax year on June 1, 2026, and stays offline until the new season opens in December 2026. That puts the next bill a few weeks away from today. Owners with a mortgage escrow account get an informational bill around mid-July instead, while the lender receives the payment copy directly.

What are the Brookhaven due dates and late charges?

The first half is due January 10 and the second half May 31. The town accepts one bill split into two payments. After the first-half date, the interest steps up each month, and the final day to pay without going delinquent is May 31.

Taxpayers who receive Enhanced STAR or the over-65 exemption get five more business days after May 31. Beyond that date, the account is delinquent and payable to the Suffolk County Comptroller, who adds a 5 percent penalty and interest of 1 percent per month counted from February 1. The town is not part of the delinquency process.

How do I pay my Brookhaven taxes?

Pay online, in person, or by mail, but watch the postmark rules. A federal change that took effect December 24, 2025 means mail dropped in a box may not get a same-day postmark. The town says the only guaranteed method is a hand-stamped envelope at a post office counter, and the tax office cannot waive penalties when a payment lacks a timely postmark.

  • Online: an e-check costs $1.75, and a credit card carries a 2.35 percent fee. Partial payments cannot be made online.
  • Drop box: outside the front lobby of Town Hall, open around the clock, no cash. A receipt is mailed the next business day.
  • Walk-in: Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
  • Mail: send the right stub with the check, postmarked by January 10 for the first half and May 31 for the second half.

Partial payments of $200 or more plus any interest are accepted by the Receiver and by the Comptroller. A returned check adds a $20 charge.

How do I grieve a Brookhaven assessment?

File between May 1 and Grievance Day, the third Tuesday in May. In 2026 that was May 19, with an online application open from May 1 until the end of that day. The next one is Tuesday, May 18, 2027.

The Assessor's calendar sets March 1 as the taxable status date, the day your exemption applications are due. The tentative roll is filed May 1, and the final roll is filed July 1. Mailed grievances must be sent to the Town of Brookhaven Assessor, Attention: Grievance, at 1 Independence Hill, or left in the Assessor's bin at the main lobby security desk. In 2026 the Assessor also kept extended hours on Thursday, May 7 from 4:30 to 8 p.m. and Saturday, May 9 from 8 a.m. to noon, and the 2026 Grievance Day hearing ran from 4 to 8 p.m. on the third floor of Town Hall in the Work Session Room. Check the Grievance Day page each spring for the 2027 schedule.

Owners who file late get nothing. The town states that applications submitted before May 1 or after the Grievance Day deadline are returned to the applicant.

What happens if I sell a Brookhaven house with taxes unpaid?

Suffolk County law makes timely payment the property owner's duty even when no bill arrived, and the owner is liable for penalties and interest on late payments. Because bills go out in December, the town tells anyone who buys in Suffolk County during the following year to call the Receiver and confirm every tax is current.

  • Sellers should ask the Receiver for a current figure and note whether the first half or the whole year is paid.
  • If the bill went to a former address, give the Receiver the right mailing address.
  • After May 31, ask the Suffolk County Comptroller for the payoff. Its check address is 330 Center Drive in Riverhead.

If taxes stay unpaid until the tax lien sale, which the town says usually happens in December, the Comptroller sells a lien to Suffolk County. A cash buyer can pay off a delinquent balance at closing the same way a lender would, which avoids that sale.

What do Brookhaven housing numbers look like?

Brookhaven is mostly owner-occupied, with about four of every five homes lived in by their owners, and the average commute runs 32.3 minutes each way. Stony Brook University and Brookhaven National Laboratory together account for roughly half of the employees at the town's top ten employers, and the Long Island Rail Road serves the area.

Census QuickFacts figures for the town (2020 to 2024 survey, 2025 estimate):

  • Population estimate, July 2025: 496,410.
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 80.9%.
  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $489,200.
  • Median gross rent: $2,314.
  • Households: 166,521.

The median household income is $120,110, and the median monthly owner cost is $3,101 with a mortgage and $1,377 without one. Total area is 531.54 square miles, of which 272.11 is water, so water makes up a little over half of the town's area. If your valuation seems out of line with similar houses nearby, call the Assessor before May.

Frequently asked questions

When are Brookhaven property taxes due?

The first half is due by January 10 and the second half by May 31. Late first-half payments add 1 percent for each month, up to 5 percent in the last three weeks of May.

Who do I pay after May 31 in Brookhaven?

The Suffolk County Comptroller, at the Suffolk County Treasurer address on Center Drive in Riverhead. A 5 percent penalty plus 1 percent a month from February 1 is added to the balance.

Can I pay Brookhaven tax by credit card?

Yes, online, with a 2.35 percent bank fee. An e-check costs $1.75. Neither fee goes to the town, and partial payments cannot be made online.

When is Brookhaven Grievance Day?

It falls on the third Tuesday in May. That was May 19 in 2026 and will be May 18 in 2027. Applications are accepted from May 1 through that day.

What if I never got a Brookhaven tax bill?

You still owe the tax and any penalties. Call the Receiver of Taxes at 631-451-9009 if the bill has not arrived by the third week of December, and keep your mailing address current.

Does Buffalo reassess property every year?

To qualify for a credit in a given year, the owner must own the property and live in it as the primary residence as of July 1 of that year. A buyer who closes after that date registers for the following year.

What if tax is still open when I sell in East Hampton?

A delinquent balance stays attached to the parcel, so it needs to be paid or settled around the time title transfers. The Comptroller's FAQ explains the sequence: if taxes are still unpaid at the tax lien sale, usually held in December, the Comptroller sells a lien to Suffolk County to cover the delinquent tax for that year.

The owner or anyone with an interest can redeem within twelve months of the sale date. Property assessed as a one, two or three-family residence gets thirty-six months. If the redemption period lapses, the county issues a tax deed, and an application to redeem after that goes to the Department of Planning, Division of Real Estate.

  • A 1% discount on the second half applies when both school halves are paid by November 10, or both general halves by February 10. The discounted figure is printed under the total box on the bill.

After a levy closes, payment goes to the Nassau County Treasurer at 1 West Street, Mineola, 516-571-2090. The county runs its own late schedule, so call before you send a check. A bill with the word "arrears" in its upper left corner means unpaid tax is already collecting penalties at the county.

A first-half school payment picks up 2% on November 11 and gains another point each month after that, reaching 8% in May. The second half has a single step: 2% from May 11 to May 31.

How can I pay a Hempstead tax bill?

You can pay in person, by mail, online, by phone or at one of several satellite points. Pick the one that gives you a dated receipt before the deadline.

  • The Receiver's office on N Franklin Street, where tax cashiers issue an immediate receipt.
  • The EZ-Pay Drive-Thru window behind the Receiver's office, plus satellite offices at Levittown Hall and Rock Hall Museum and a mobile tax office. These give a temporary receipt, and the final one is mailed within seven business days.
  • Online or by phone with a card or electronic check through the Receiver's Payment Center.
  • Mail, with the number 1 stub for a first half, the number 2 stub for a second half, or both stubs for the full year.

Card payments carry a 2.3% convenience fee with a $1.50 minimum. Visa debit is a flat $3.95, and an e-check costs $0.90. The fees go to the payment processor, eGov Strategies, and not to the town. A mailed payment only counts if it has an official U.S. Postal Service cancellation date on or before the last penalty-free day, because a metered postmark is not accepted. Owners aged 65 or older, or with a disability, who own a one to three family home can name a third party to receive a duplicate bill.

Who sets a Hempstead assessment, and when can I challenge it?

Nassau County sets your assessment, and the town does not. The county's Assessment Review Commission is an agency separate from the Department of Assessment, and it takes appeals online through a system called AROW. The commission sits at 240 Old Country Road, 5th Floor, Mineola, and answers at 516-571-3214.

The county's date table puts the next tentative roll on January 4, 2027, with grievances due March 1, 2027. The final roll follows on April 3, 2028, and court petitions are due May 1, 2028. That roll feeds the 2028/29 school year and the 2029 town and county bills. New York State's grievance page confirms that Nassau complaints are due March 1 and that filing costs nothing and needs no lawyer.

If the commission denies your complaint, a Small Claims Assessment Review is open to owners who live in a one, two or three family home. The state lists a $30 filing fee and a 30 day window after the final roll is filed.

Which exemptions can lower a Hempstead bill?

The town lists six programs: senior citizens, veterans, disability or limited income, STAR, home improvement, and volunteer firefighters and ambulance personnel. Applications go to the Nassau County Department of Assessment, which accepts them year-round, and the filing deadline is January 2. Call 516-571-1500 for forms.

STAR works differently for new applicants. They register with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance and receive a credit check, not a bill reduction. The Receiver also runs tax forums around the town on exemptions, challenges and early-payment discounts, and sellers who have never claimed anything may find a missed program worth checking before listing.

What happens to Hempstead property tax when I sell?

Unpaid tax stays attached to the parcel until someone pays it, so the sale needs a payoff figure. Settle these items before the closing date:

  • Ask the Receiver at 516-538-1500 which halves of the School and General bills are paid.
  • If a bill shows "arrears," call the Nassau County Treasurer at 516-571-2090 for the amount, since the Receiver no longer holds that tax.
  • Expect exemptions to drop off at transfer. The Department of Assessment removes any exemption a new owner does not qualify for, which is why a buyer's bill can differ a lot from yours.
  • Have the new owner send the ownership and mortgage change form to the Receiver. The town warns owners not to assume an attorney or lender will do it.

A cash purchase can build the tax payoff into the closing statement, so the money never has to come out of your pocket first. If you are behind on Hempstead tax and a lender or lien is involved, get a written payoff from each office first.

What is the Hempstead housing market like for sellers?

Hempstead village is dense and mostly renter-heavy. Census QuickFacts for the village lists 17,108 households at 3.37 people each. Owners occupy 47.5% of homes, the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $459,500, rent runs $1,622 at the median, and household income sits at $90,420. The village covers 3.69 square miles and had an estimated 59,819 residents in July 2025.

The wider town is the most populous in New York State, at 793,409 people in the 2020 census. Hofstra University's campus is in Hempstead, the Long Island Rail Road's Hempstead Branch ends here, and Hempstead Turnpike (NY 24) and the Southern State Parkway tie the area to the rest of Nassau County. Houses here sell on their own tax bill and condition, so a fresh payoff letter helps more than a neighborhood average.

Frequently asked questions

Where do I pay Hempstead property tax in person?

At the Receiver of Taxes, 200 N Franklin Street, First Floor, Hempstead, NY 11550. The drive-thru window behind the building and the satellite offices at Levittown Hall and Rock Hall Museum also take payments.

Can I still pay school tax to the Hempstead Receiver after May 31?

No. School tax can be paid to the Receiver through May 31, and general tax through August 31. After that, payment goes to the Nassau County Treasurer at 1 West Street in Mineola, 516-571-2090.

Does the Town of Hempstead set my assessment?

No. Nassau County sets assessments, and appeals go to the county's Assessment Review Commission. The next tentative roll is dated January 4, 2027, and grievances are due March 1, 2027.

Will my exemptions pass to the buyer of my Hempstead house?

No. When title transfers, the Nassau County Department of Assessment removes exemptions the new owner is not entitled to. The buyer's first bill can be much higher than yours.

What does it mean if my Hempstead bill says arrears?

It means unpaid tax is already accruing penalties at the Nassau County Treasurer's office. Contact the Treasurer at 516-571-2090 before you pay anything, because the county uses a different penalty schedule than the town.

Counter hours for payments are 9 am to 4 pm, Monday through Friday. The general office stays open from 8 am to 5:30 pm.

Huntington sends one bill a year, in the second week of December. For 2026/27, the town lists January 10, 2027 for the first half and May 31, 2027 for the second. A due date on a weekend slides forward, and Town Hall lists extended payment hours until 7 pm on June 1, 2027. January 10, 2027 itself falls on a Sunday.

Two groups get extra days on the second half. Owners receiving Basic STAR have until June 4, 2027. So do seniors on the Senior Low-Income exemption or Enhanced STAR, though after June 1 they can only pay by mail or at the counter.

Because of a federal postmark change effective December 24, 2025, a mailbox drop may not receive a same-day postmark. What is the Huntington grievance process?

Basic and Enhanced STAR are state programs. For questions, call the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance at 518-457-2036.

Huntington sits on the North Shore of Long Island, with Long Island Sound to the north and Nassau County to the west. It was founded in 1653, and the arrival of the Long Island Rail Road in 1867 turned a farming and shipping town into a commuter base. The town covers 94.0 square miles of land. Its four incorporated villages are Asharoken, Huntington Bay, Lloyd Harbor and Northport, and hamlets include Dix Hills, Melville, Commack, Greenlawn and Huntington Station.

Household income reaches $168,029, median rent is $2,358, and workers spend 35.2 minutes getting to work on average. Major employers named in the town's 2025 budget include Canon, the Northport VA Medical Center and Huntington Hospital.

School districts named for the town's communities include Cold Spring Harbor, Elwood, Half Hollow Hills, Harborfields, Huntington, South Huntington and Northport-East Northport,.

Send it to the Suffolk County Comptroller at 330 Center Drive, Riverhead, NY 11901. The comptroller's number is (631) 852-3000, and the amount includes a 5% penalty plus monthly interest.

Grievance Day lands on the third Tuesday of May, so May 18 in 2027. The Assessor's Office must receive an originally signed complaint on or before that day, and fax or email copies are rejected.

How does property tax collection work in Islip, NY?

Islip collects through its Receiver of Taxes on a December to May cycle. An owner who cannot pay in full can split it, with the first half due January 10 and the second half due May 31.

Islip mails one bill a year. If a lender escrows your tax, you will not receive the December bill and will get a statement in February after the first half is paid and again in July after the second. A bill that never arrives is no excuse, because state law keeps the owner responsible, and the town cannot waive a penalty.

The 2025-2026 collection ended June 1, 2026. The 2026-2027 tax year begins on December 1, 2026, and the town says details for it will be posted in early to mid December 2026. Taxes become a lien on December 1 of each year. Nobody can pay early, because the Receiver does not know the amount until the warrant arrives from the Suffolk County Legislature.

The Town Assessor's Office at 40 Nassau Avenue values more than 99,000 parcels and also approves exemptions. The office phone is (631) 224-5585.

The tentative roll can be inspected at the Assessor's Office. In 2026 the schedule ran weekdays from May 1 to May 15, 8:30 am to 5 pm, then 9 am to 1 pm on Saturday May 16, 8:30 am to 8 pm on May 18 and 8:30 am to 9 pm on Grievance Day.   • Assessment estimates: on written request, the office gives a one-year estimate before you add a pool, bathroom or addition.

For the 2027/28 year, applications with 2025 income proof are due by March 1, 2027. Seniors apply at Suite 2 (631-224-5058) and persons with disabilities at Suite 3 (631-224-5585).

Basic STAR covers owner-occupied primary homes where the owners and spouses earn less than $250,000, and it removes the first $30,000 of full value from school tax. Enhanced STAR serves owners aged 65 and up with income under $113,550 for 2027/28, and the state will upgrade Basic to Enhanced automatically. For STAR help call the state at 518-457-2036.

What should I know about Islip property tax before selling?

Because tax is a lien from December 1, a sale between December and May needs a payoff for the current year. Ask the Receiver where the bill stands, and then check the title company's search for earlier years.

  • If the bill shows the word RESTORATION, the prior owner had exemptions the buyer cannot keep, and the buyer repays them once, in that tax year.
  • Owners who finish paying a mortgage should call the Receiver so the records change.
  • The mailing address change form sits in the Forms section of the town site.

A cash buyer can take a house with an open tax balance and pay it from the closing proceeds, so penalties stop stacking while the sale is pending. If the house has a senior or disability exemption, tell the buyer early so the restoration amount is not a surprise.

Islip is a South Shore town in Suffolk County, incorporated in 1683. It covers 103.2 square miles of land, borders the Atlantic to the south, and includes part of Fire Island, Jones Beach Island and Captree Island. Villages are Brightwaters, Islandia, Ocean Beach and Saltaire, and hamlets include Bay Shore, Brentwood, Central Islip, Sayville, West Islip and Ronkonkoma. Long Island MacArthur Airport, which the town owns, sits in Ronkonkoma, and Fire Island ferries leave from Bay Shore and Sayville.

Median household income is $130,132, and 36.6% of residents speak a language other than English at home. The Long Island Rail Road's Montauk Branch serves Bay Shore through Sayville, and the Main Line serves Brentwood, Central Islip and Ronkonkoma.

No. The Receiver does not know the amounts until the warrant comes from the Suffolk County Legislature in early December.

To the Suffolk County Comptroller, 330 Center Drive, Riverhead, NY 11901. The phone number is (631) 852-3000, and penalty and interest are added.

It is the third Tuesday in May, so May 18, 2027. A complaint must reach the Assessor's Office by 9 pm that day or the Board of Assessment Review dismisses it as untimely.

The school and library year runs July to June while the city and county bills follow the calendar year. A closing date that falls mid-year therefore lands in a different slice of each bill. Ask the closing attorney or title company to adjust each of the four bills separately.

Which office sends the New Rochelle tax bill?

The City of New Rochelle Tax Department sends the bills and takes the payments for the city, Westchester County, the New Rochelle City School District and the New Rochelle Public Library. Assessments come from a different office, the Bureau of Assessments inside the Finance Department, which prepares the assessment roll that every one of those bills is built on.

  • Assessor's Office: 515 North Avenue, New Rochelle, NY 10801, weekday hours of 8:30 am until 4:30 pm, telephone (914) 654-2052.
  • Online: the city runs a payment portal that accepts cards and e-checks. Convenience fees apply.
  • In person: the Tax Office is on the ground floor of City Hall at the same North Avenue address.
  • By mail: payable to Tax Collector New Rochelle, with the block and lot number written on the check. The city advises against paying through personal online banking.
  • Direct debit: the city can draw payments automatically from a checking or money market account once you return its authorization form.

Two web tools show parcel data. CitySquared offers mapping, parcel basics and building permit information, and the SDG Property Information portal adds photos and tax history. The city site does not publish a single tax rate for homeowners, so ask the Tax Department about the rate on your own parcel.

What is it like to own and sell a house in New Rochelle?

New Rochelle sits on Long Island Sound at the southeastern point of continental New York, about two miles north of Pelham Bay Park in the Bronx. The city is shaped like a long triangle, roughly ten miles from north to south and 1.5 miles across at its widest, and its land and water together measure 13.2 square miles.

French Huguenot families founded the settlement in 1688, and the village and town merged into one city under a charter signed in 1899. Planned neighborhoods such as Rochelle Park earned it the nickname "City of Homes." The Metro-North station and the New Roc City complex downtown are products of the late twentieth century rebuilding.

Census Bureau The current picture for a seller:

  • Population estimated at 85,864 on July 1, 2025, up 7.7 percent from the 2020 base.
  • 31,684 households, with 53.7 percent of housing units owner-occupied.
  • A typical owned home valued at $702,500 over 2020 to 2024, with gross rent at a median of $1,917.
  • Average commute of 32.5 minutes each way.

Water is part of life here. The city has a page for owners with chronic flooding, and an owner whose home is damaged enough to lower its value, with repairs not done by December 1, can contact the assessor in April to arrange an inspection.

How does the New Rochelle assessment calendar work?

The year turns on December 1, the taxable status date. Every property is assessed on its condition that day, and December 1 is also the deadline for filing exemption applications with the Assessor's Office, in person or by mail to 515 North Avenue.

  • December 1: taxable status date and exemption deadline.
  • February 1: the tentative assessment roll is published.
  • Third Tuesday in February: Grievance Day.
  • April 1: the final assessment roll. A changed assessment shows up in the billing cycle that begins September 1.

The city has not run a citywide reassessment since 1956, so values on the roll rarely track the market sale prices you see around town. Renovations are the exception. Work finished in a given year is reviewed as of that year's December 1 and any new figure appears on the next February roll. A homeowner planning a kitchen or an addition before listing can ask the City Appraiser for an estimate of the effect.

How do I file a grievance on my New Rochelle assessment?

File Form RP-524 with the Assessor's Office between February 1 and the third Tuesday in February. The city's grievance page says applications outside that window cannot be accepted.

  • Look at your tentative roll entry on or after February 1, which shows the assessed value and the assessor's estimate of market value.
  • Gather at least three recent arm's length sales of similar homes close by, matched on size, style, age, condition and lot.
  • Submit the original application in person or by mail. Email and fax copies are refused.
  • File one application for each parcel if you own more than one or your property spans several lots.
  • Ask the Assessor's Office for a hearing time with the Board of Assessment Review after the form is in.

The board is made up of residents appointed by the City Council, and no assessor staff sit on it. If your assessment is fair but the bill still feels heavy, the assessor cannot help, since tax rates are set by the council, the school district and the county legislature. After the grievance stage, New York offers Small Claims Assessment Review to most homeowners, and the state says you must go through the local grievance first.

Which exemptions and STAR benefits apply in New Rochelle?

A new owner who applies for STAR receives it as a check or direct deposit from the state. You register with New York State at tax.ny.gov/star, and the credit requires a primary residence and combined income of all owners and spouses of $500,000 or less.

The older Basic STAR exemption stays in place for people who applied before May 1, 2015, with a combined income under $250,000, and its savings have been capped since 2019. Enhanced STAR is for owners 65 or older within the state income limit, and the state now moves eligible owners over without a new application. Other exemptions are filed with the New Rochelle assessor by December 1.

When you sell, the state asks you to close your STAR registration. Your buyer registers as a new owner of the home.

What happens to unpaid New Rochelle tax when I sell?

Open balances have to be settled as part of the sale, so start by asking the Tax Department for a statement of every unpaid bill on the parcel. Check the city's fee lists as well, because unpaid false alarm charges move onto the next city tax bill after September 30, and restored to roll, sidewalk repair and property maintenance charges move over after December 1.

The deed itself is recorded with the Westchester County Clerk, not at City Hall. The city assessor says ownership records cannot be changed at the city level and points owners to an attorney who files the papers with the county clerk. If you are behind on taxes, tell your closing attorney or title company early so the payoff figures are ready before the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

Which office handles New Rochelle assessment questions?

The Assessor's Office at 515 North Avenue, which can be reached at (914) 654-2052 on weekdays. It answers questions about assessed value, exemptions and grievance forms but has no say over the tax rate.

When is Grievance Day in New Rochelle?

It falls on the third Tuesday in February. Applications can be filed from February 1 through that Tuesday, and the tentative roll comes out on February 1.

Can I pay a New Rochelle tax bill with a credit card?

Yes, through the city's online payment portal, which also takes e-checks. Convenience fees apply. You can also pay at the City Hall Tax Office, by mail or by direct debit.

Is the New Rochelle school tax due once a year?

No. It is split into two halves, due on or before September 30 and March 31. The library bill rides along with the school bill.

Who pays the March school installment if I sell in the winter?

That depends on your contract and the closing adjustments. The March bill covers January through June, so ask your attorney how the closing statement will divide it.

What is the property tax rate in New York City for 2026?

New York City sets one rate for each of four tax classes, and the 2026 rates run from 10.848 percent to 19.843 percent of taxable value. A typical house, with one to three dwelling units, falls in Class 1, which carries the highest rate of the four.

New York City tax year 2026 rates by class, from the Department of Finance rate table
ClassWhat it coversRate
Class 1One to three unit residential property19.843%
Class 2Larger residential buildings, co-ops and condos12.439%
Class 3Mostly utility property11.108%
Class 4Mostly commercial property10.848%

Source: NYC Department of Finance, property tax rates, and the Notice of Property Value page for the class descriptions.

Who assesses and bills property tax in New York City?

The Department of Finance does both jobs. It values every parcel each year, mails the bills and collects the payments, while an independent body called the Tax Commission hears appeals. The city covers all five boroughs, Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Staten Island, under a single tax system with no separate county or town collectors.

The city's bills carry a real weight in its budget. The Department of Finance reports that property tax made up 41 percent of all city tax dollars collected in the fiscal year that ended June 30, 2026.

  • You receive a bill if you pay the tax yourself and have a balance. If a bank or mortgage company pays through escrow, the bill goes to them.
  • Bills are usually mailed and posted online about a month before they are due.
  • Owners remain responsible for paying on time even when no bill arrives, so keep your mailing address current with the department.
  • Water and sewer charges come from the Department of Environmental Protection and are billed apart from the tax.

The Census Bureau's QuickFacts sizes up the market: an estimated 8,584,629 residents in July 2025 across 300.45 square miles of land, 3,334,088 households, and an owner-occupied rate of only 32.8 percent. Owned homes carry a median value of $777,600, and the median gross rent is $1,821.

When are New York City property taxes due?

The city's fiscal year opens each July 1 and closes the next June 30, and how often you pay depends on the assessed value of the property. Under the Department of Finance's due dates page, a property assessed at $250,000 or less is billed four times a year, and one assessed above $250,000 is billed twice.

  • Quarterly payers: the first of July, October, January and April, each with an interest-free grace period through the 15th of the month.
  • Semi-annual payers: July 1 and January 1.
  • Weekends and holidays: a due date on one rolls to the following business day.
  • Mailed payments: the postmark date counts.

Paying ahead earns a discount. Settling the whole year's tax by the July due date or grace date takes 0.50 percent off. Paying the remaining three quarters by October 15 earns 0.33 percent, and paying the final six months by January 15 earns 0.17 percent. Late payment interest is required by law and compounds daily.

How is a New York City assessment worked out?

The Department of Finance starts with market value, converts it to an assessed value that is a percentage of that figure, subtracts any exemptions to reach taxable value, multiplies by the class rate, and then subtracts abatements. The result is your yearly bill.

The Notice of Property Value arrives in January each year. It is not a bill and requires no payment. State law limits how far some assessments can move in a single year, so an assessment can take several years to catch up with the market. The department's own example for a one to three family home shows a market value that jumps from $100,000 to $150,000 while the assessed value moves only from 6,000 to 6,360.

Selling a house usually settles the question of market value, but the assessment is a separate number. A buyer will look at what the next bill will be, so know your current class, exemptions and any abatement before you list.

How do I challenge a New York City assessment?

File an application for correction with the Tax Commission. The deadline is March 15 for Class 1 properties and March 1 for Classes 2, 3 and 4, and the department says late appeals will not be granted.

  • Read the Notice of Property Value first. If it shows an "effective market value," you must show your market value is lower than that figure to win.
  • A Request for Review sent to the Department of Finance is a different step. It covers description errors and is due March 15 for Class 1 and April 1 for other classes.
  • A Request for Review does not replace a timely Tax Commission filing.
  • A Request to Update corrects stale facts such as unit counts or vacant land descriptions.

The Commission can lower an assessment, change a tax class and adjust exemptions. A seller who plans to list in spring should mark these two March dates on the calendar, because the decision affects the tax a buyer inherits.

Can New York City sell a lien on my house for unpaid tax?

Yes, if the debt passes the minimum for your property type. A lien sale transfers the debt to an authorized buyer, not the house itself, but the new lienholder can start a foreclosure if the balance stays unpaid. The city's lien sales page says the most recent sale was held on June 3, 2025.

For an owner-occupied one-family home, the property tax debt must be at least $5,000 and three years overdue. Two and three family homes follow that rule and can also be listed for $3,000 or more in water and sewer charges outstanding for a year. A one-family owner who owes only water and sewer charges cannot have a lien sold.

  • Homes with a Senior Citizen Homeowners' or Disabled Homeowners' exemption are excluded, as are combat and disabled veterans' properties and those with the State Circuit Breaker. STAR does not protect a property.
  • After a sale, the lienholder may add a 5 percent surcharge, interest of 6, 9 or 16 percent by assessed value, and about $300 in notice costs.
  • Foreclosure can begin within a year of the sale, or sooner if a semi-annual interest payment is more than 30 days late.
  • A waiver of the 5 percent surcharge exists for a primary residence owner with no other city property and combined income of $110,750 or less.

Is there a payment plan if I owe New York City property tax?

The Department of Finance offers a standard plan, a deferral program for eligible homeowners called PT AID, and a reduced interest plan for some Class 1 owners. The standard plan allows monthly or quarterly payments for up to 10 years, with no required down payment, although paying something up front lowers each installment.

Interest is set by law and depends on assessed value. For the year that ended June 30, 2026, the rates were 6 percent at $250,000 or less, 9 percent up to $450,000 and 16 percent above that, with 2.5 percent for the reduced interest plan. Ask the department for the rate now in force. A plan cannot be opened once a lien sale or an in rem action has already taken place on the property.

Which transfer taxes apply to a New York City sale?

Tax at closing is more than the property tax bill. New York State charges a transfer tax of $2 for each $500 of price, paid by the seller, and every New York City conveyance is reported on Form TP-584-NYC, according to the state Tax Department. The buyer pays the 1 percent mansion tax when a residence sells for $1 million or more.

Homes at the upper end carry added city taxes. A residential sale of $3 million or more triggers an extra base tax of $1.25 per $500 paid by the seller, and a supplemental buyer tax of 0.25 to 2.9 percent applies from $2 million. A separate surcharge on high value second homes took effect May 28, 2026, and the department has published a supplemental roll of parcels that might be affected. Ask your closing attorney to request a current statement of what you owe before the closing date.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Class 1 tax rate in New York City?

It is 19.843 percent for tax year 2026. That rate is applied to taxable value, which is a fraction of market value after exemptions.

Is the Notice of Property Value a tax bill?

No. It arrives each January and shows how the Department of Finance valued the property. No payment is due with it.

By when must a Class 1 appeal be filed?

March 15, to the Tax Commission. For Classes 2, 3 and 4 the date is March 1.

Does paying early save money in New York City?

Yes. The full year paid by the July due date or grace date earns 0.50 percent. Paying the rest of the year in October earns 0.33 percent, and in January 0.17 percent.

Will a lien sale take my house?

The sale transfers the debt, not the property. If the new lienholder is not paid or no agreement is reached, a foreclosure case can follow, usually a year after the sale.

Who bills property tax in the Town of North Hempstead?

The Town's Receiver of Taxes bills and collects school and general tax for the Town of North Hempstead, and the Nassau County Department of Assessment sets the assessments behind the bills. The town's site names Mary Jo Collins as Receiver of Taxes, and the office sits at 200 Plandome Road in Manhasset, open Monday to Friday from 9:00 a.m. to 4:45 p.m.

The town covers about 54 square miles of land in Nassau County and had an estimated 238,982 residents on July 1, 2025, according to the Census Bureau. Roughly 79.5% of homes are owner-occupied, and the 2020-2024 figure for median owner-occupied value is $888,000.

What are the North Hempstead property tax due dates?

School tax and general tax run on separate calendars. The school year is July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027, and the general tax year is January 1, 2027 to December 31, 2027. If the 10th lands on a weekend or holiday, the penalty-free deadline moves to the next business day.

The November 10 deadline for the first school half has already gone by as of mid-November 2026. If that bill is still open, the unpaid amount is moving toward the county's delinquent roll, so call the Receiver's office for a current figure.

How do you pay a North Hempstead tax bill?

You can pay online, by phone, by mail, or in person. The town accepts electronic checks, major credit cards, and Visa or Mastercard debit cards through its payment vendor.

  • Electronic check costs a $1.75 flat fee, a credit card costs 2.3% of the amount, and a Visa or Mastercard debit card costs a $3.95 flat fee. State law requires the payer to bear card fees.
  • Mailed payments go to the Receiver of Taxes at the Manhasset post office box printed on the bill, and the envelope must be postmarked by the due date.
  • The office has an after-hours dropbox for checks and money orders, and a kiosk handles card payments inside.
  • For the first-half 2026-27 school bill, the town also ran collection tables at parks and community centers in October.

The town warns that since December 24, 2025 a USPS postmark reflects the date a regional facility processed the mail, so a letter mailed close to a deadline can pick up a later postmark. Real Property Law section 925 does not allow a late penalty to be waived, and taxes count as paid only after the payment clears the bank.

Which school districts and villages affect a North Hempstead bill?

Your school tax goes to the district that serves your address, and your village, if you live in one, bills its own tax on top. The town's closing guide lists these district codes: Westbury, East Williston, Roslyn, Port Washington, New Hyde Park, Manhasset, Great Neck, Herricks, Mineola, Carle Place, Floral Park, Glenwood Landing and Jericho.

More than two dozen incorporated villages sit inside the town, among them Great Neck Plaza, Kings Point, Lake Success, Manorhaven, Munsey Park, Plandome, Roslyn Harbor, Russell Gardens, Saddle Rock, Sands Point, Thomaston and Williston Park. A village collects its own taxes and can use assessed values that differ from the county roll, so a seller in a village should also ask the village clerk for a balance and due date. A dispute over which district a house belongs to goes to that district or the state education commissioner, because the town has no say.

How does the school and general tax split affect a sale?

Each half-year bill covers a different slice of time, so the seller and buyer settle up based on which months each bill paid for. Per the Receiver's closing guide, the first-half school levy covers July 1 to December 31, the second-half school levy covers January 1 to June 30, the first-half general levy covers January 1 to June 30, and the second-half general levy covers July 1 to December 31.

The town's guide tells closing parties to match the closing date to these periods. A sale in November, for example, falls inside the first school half and the second general half, and a sale in April sits in the second school half and the first general half. Ask your attorney or title company for a written payoff before closing, and near a deadline ask the town for the exact penalty figure.

What happens to exemptions and restored taxes after a sale?

Exemptions generally do not move with the deed, and the buyer applies on their own with the Nassau County Department of Assessment. If an exemption ends because of a sale, Nassau County may add prorated restored taxes of up to one year to a later bill, and because of the county assessment calendar this can take up to two years to show up.

New owners must tell the Receiver of Taxes, and the incorporated village if there is one, about the new ownership, mailing address and mortgage escrow, which keeps bills from going to the wrong place. Improvements, including work done before a sale that was never reported, can raise the assessed value beyond the 6% cap.

The town also describes these programs, which the county administers:

  • STAR, which applies only to school tax. Basic STAR is open to all ages with income of $500,000 or less, and Enhanced STAR is for owners 65 and older.
  • A senior citizens exemption reducing county, town and school tax by 5% to 65% on a sliding income scale, with the top 65% tier at $47,000 of income or less.
  • Disability, veterans, and volunteer firefighter and ambulance exemptions.
  • A home improvement exemption that decreases over eight years on qualifying work.

The statewide STAR rules are covered in our New York STAR guide.

How do you challenge a North Hempstead assessment?

File an application for correction with the Nassau County Assessment Review Commission, which is separate from the Department of Assessment. The Commission says the next window follows the tentative roll set January 4, 2027, with filing open through March 1, 2027, and the town's own page lists January 2 as the opening date, so check which date the Commission shows when you file.

You can file online through AROW, in person at 240 Old Country Road in Mineola, or by asking for a paper form. There is no filing fee, and you may represent yourself or hire a representative. The Commission asks for sales of comparable homes, and its online sales locator helps you find them. If the Commission denies the appeal, a Small Claims Assessment Review petition in court is the next step. The Receiver of Taxes does not set assessments and cannot change them, and a village that keeps its own roll requires a separate filing with the Village Assessor.

What if North Hempstead property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid tax moves to the Nassau County Treasurer. For the towns of Hempstead, North Hempstead and Oyster Bay, the Treasurer's Tax Records department handles both delinquent general and school tax, starting June 1 for school tax and September 1 for general tax.

The county's page for 2026 delinquent taxes shows personal checks accepted from June 1 to November 30, 2026, credit card and electronic check payments from June 26, 2026 through January 31, 2027, and Wednesday, February 10, 2027 at 3:00 PM as the last day to pay before the lien sale. Tax liens themselves cannot be paid online and need a bank cashier's check or cash.

The state's lien and foreclosure rules are in our tax lien guide. If you plan to sell a house with unpaid tax, ask for a payoff in writing and have your closing attorney pay it from the proceeds. Your bill shows the rate for your parcel, and the Receiver's office can answer questions about it.

Frequently asked questions

When is North Hempstead general tax due?

The first half of the 2027 general tax is due January 1, 2027, and can be paid without penalty through February 10, 2027. The second half is due July 1, 2027, with a penalty-free deadline of August 10, 2027.

Where do I pay my North Hempstead taxes in person?

At the Receiver of Taxes office, 200 Plandome Road in Manhasset, Monday to Friday from 9:00 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. Bring your bill. Card payments go through the kiosk, and checks or money orders can use the after-hours dropbox.

Is the November 10, 2026 school tax deadline still open?

No. It passed on November 10, 2026, and the first-half school bill is late if still unpaid. Contact the Receiver's office about penalties, and expect delinquent amounts to be collected by the Nassau County Treasurer.

Who do I call to appeal my assessment?

The Nassau County Assessment Review Commission handles appeals, and its page lists a phone line for paper forms and questions. The Receiver of Taxes does not set or change assessments.

Do I keep my STAR benefit if I sell and move?

Not on the house you sold. The Tax Department says to close the registration when you sell, and your buyer should register for the STAR credit once the home is their primary residence.

Who sends the property tax bill for a house in Rochester?

The City of Rochester sends one bill that covers the city and the Rochester City School District, and Monroe County sends a second bill. A house inside the city limits therefore carries two separate tax accounts, and a buyer or title company will ask about both.

The city's tax billing page says bills go out by mail each July to owners who do not pay through a mortgage escrow. It also repeats a rule from New York Real Property Tax Law section 922: the owner still has to pay on time if a bill never arrives. Monroe County bills separately and mails its bill on December 31 for city properties, according to the city's tax rates page. For county questions the city page points owners to the Monroe County Real Property Tax Service Office.

Three city offices matter if you are about to sell:

  • Bureau of Assessment, City Hall Room 101A, 30 Church Street: values, exemptions and assessment complaints.
  • Treasury Bureau, City Hall, 30 Church Street: unpaid taxes, payment agreements and the amount owed on a given parcel.
  • Rochester Water Department and the Municipal Code Violations Bureau: water charges and code fines, which the city says its online property tool does not show in full.

When are the four Rochester tax installments due?

Rochester splits the city and school bill into four installments: July 31, September 30, January 31 and March 31. The city's treasury page lists the 2026 cycle as July 31 and September 30, 2026, then January 31 and March 31, 2027. Two of those dates have already passed this year, so check whether a balance rolled forward before you list the house.

A late installment starts to collect interest at 1 percent per month. If a deadline lands on a weekend, the following Monday is the cutoff. The city encourages electronic payment, and mailed payments now go to a Binghamton post office box named on the bill coupon, with the check made out to the City Treasurer and the installment coupon enclosed. Payments under a tax agreement are the exception: those go straight to the Treasury Bureau at City Hall.

The city mailing address changed on July 1, 2026, so an old return label from a prior year should be thrown away. An owner paying in full by July 31 should send the first installment coupon, because the city built that coupon to handle either a full payment or the first quarter.

What are the 2026-27 Rochester tax rates for a home?

A one, two or three family house in Rochester is taxed at the homestead rate, which for 2026-27 combines to $18.2157 per $1,000 of assessed value once city, school, county and the Pure Waters capital charge are added. Everything that is not a one to three family home or some vacant land pays the non-homestead rate.

How do I contest a Rochester assessment?

File a complaint with the Rochester Board of Assessment Review by 8 p.m. Eastern on the third Tuesday in March. In 2027 that Tuesday is March 16, and the form has to be received at the Bureau of Assessment, City Hall Room 101A, by that hour.

The city's assessment calendar gives the full yearly sequence:

  • February 1: exemption applications and renewals are due, and the taxable status date falls here.
  • March 1: the tentative roll is filed with New York State.
  • Third Tuesday in March: complaint deadline. Hearings run through March and April.
  • May 1: the final roll is filed.
  • May 30: Small Claims Assessment Review filing deadline.
  • July 1 through January 1: informal assessment reviews are available.

The informal review window is the quiet option for an owner who missed the March deadline. Bring photos and a recent appraisal or comparable sales if you want the assessor to look at condition problems.

Which exemptions can Rochester homeowners apply for?

The city lists STAR, a senior citizen exemption, veterans exemptions, a disability exemption, a capital improvement exemption and a clergy exemption, and every application has to reach the Bureau of Assessment by February 1, 2027. The Bureau runs an exemption hotline at 585-428-6994.

The city's exemptions page sets these thresholds:

  • Enhanced STAR: owner age 65 or older, or turning 65 by December 31, 2027, with household income up to $113,550 in 2025.
  • Senior citizen exemption: owner age 65 or older (or a surviving spouse 62 or older) with income up to $58,400 in the prior year, renewed each year.
  • Disability exemption: same $58,400 income cap, for owners receiving certain disability benefits or certified as legally blind.
  • Capital improvement: one and two family houses with at least $3,000 of qualifying improvements.

New STAR recipients get a check from New York State instead of a bill reduction, so they register with the state tax department. A seller who has been receiving a senior or disability exemption should know that the city can add a supplemental tax when a prior owner's exemption ends through a transfer or death.

What happens to unpaid Rochester taxes, and are liens still sold?

Rochester has not sold tax liens since 2020, when it suspended the program until further notice, but the lien itself still exists. A lien starts when the annual tax is levied, and once the bill has gone unpaid for one year it counts as delinquent.

When the city ran its sales, an owner got a notice and had twenty days to clear the debt, and a buyer of the lien (the city used American Tax Funding Services) collected the debt from then on. Owners could apply for a delinquency agreement with the Director of Finance at least twenty days before a sale date. Liens did not qualify for sale if a payment agreement was in force, if bankruptcy law restricted enforcement, or if a tax certiorari proceeding for the same year was pending. The state redemption rule for delinquent liens is a two-year period under RPTL section 1110, which a taxing district can lengthen for homes.

The Treasury Bureau handles delinquency questions at 585-428-6940. Ask it for a payoff figure in writing before you accept an offer on a house with unpaid years.

How do unpaid Rochester taxes get settled when I sell the house?

Your title company asks the Treasury Bureau for the amount owed and pays it from your sale proceeds at closing, so a delinquent balance does not block a sale. The balance does reduce what you receive.

The city warns that its online property information tool is updated nightly and should not be relied on for final billings or closings, because unbilled taxes, fines and fees may exist. Three separate calls cover the gaps: the Treasury Bureau for taxes, the Water Department at 585-428-5990 for water, and the Municipal Code Violations Bureau for fines and tickets. If the house has inherited or exemption history, mention that to the title company early so a supplemental tax does not surprise anyone.

For a sale where you want to skip repairs, that list is also your pre-listing checklist. A buyer paying cash for the house as it stands still needs a clean payoff letter, and getting it before the contract is signed shortens the closing.

What do Census figures show about housing in Rochester?

Rochester is a renter-heavy city: the Census Bureau's QuickFacts table shows an owner-occupied rate of 38.1 percent for 2020-2024. The July 2025 population estimate is 206,108, down 2.4 percent from the April 2020 base.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $139,600.
  • Median gross rent: $1,081.
  • Households: 93,261, averaging 2.14 people each.
  • Median household income: $47,213.
  • Land area: 35.77 square miles, about 5,909 people per square mile in 2020.

Those averages cover the whole city. The Wikipedia entry on Rochester counts 35 neighborhoods defined through the city's Celebrate City Living program and notes lake effect snow averaging just over 100 inches a year, which is worth remembering when a buyer's inspector looks at roofs and gutters. Values on a Browncroft or Charlotte street can look very different from the citywide median.

Frequently asked questions

Do I owe Monroe County tax on a Rochester house?

Yes. Rochester properties get a Monroe County bill in addition to the city and school bill, and the county bill is issued on December 31. The city bill does not include county charges, so call the Monroe County Real Property Tax Service Office at 585-753-1125 for county balances.

Can I sell a Rochester house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. The unpaid amount, with interest at 1 percent per month on late installments, is paid from your proceeds at closing. Ask the Treasury Bureau for a current payoff before you accept an offer.

Is there a way to pay overdue Rochester taxes over time?

Yes. The Director of Finance can approve a delinquency or tax agreement for eligible owners, and a parcel under an active agreement is protected from lien sale. Call the Treasury Bureau at 585-428-6940 to ask whether you qualify.

Which Rochester exemption deadline is next?

February 1, 2027, a Monday. Exemption applications and renewals, including STAR-related items for seniors, veterans and disabled owners, must be at the Bureau of Assessment by then.

What is the deadline to challenge my Rochester assessment?

8 p.m. Eastern on the third Tuesday in March, which is March 16, 2027, with the form received at City Hall Room 101A. Missing it leaves informal review between July 1 and January 1 and a Small Claims Assessment Review filing by May 30.

When are Schenectady tax bills issued and due?

Schenectady issues its tax bills on January 1 of each year, and they are payable quarterly in January, April, July and October. That is a different rhythm from Rochester, Albany or most towns, where the bill arrives in summer or autumn.

  • Hand-delivered forms get a photocopy of the first page as the receipt.
  • The board reads every application received during the period, even if you never appear in person, and skipping the hearing does not count against you.

What does the Schenectady assessment roll tell a seller?

Property class codes on the roll read 210 for a single family house, 220 for two family, 230 for three family and 280 for a multiple residence. Ask for a payoff in writing, and ask the school district for its own figure, since school taxes are collected separately.

The closing agent requests payoff amounts from the Bureau of Receipts and the school district and pays them from the sale price, so owing tax does not stop a sale. It only lowers your net.

The city bill folds in water, sewer and the trash fee, which means an old utility balance can sit inside what looks like a tax figure. Read the breakdown line by line. If a quarter has just come due, ask whether the closing agent will treat it as owed by you or prorate it with the buyer.

Who collects property tax in Smithtown, and who sets the amount?

The Town of Smithtown Receiver of Taxes collects every real property tax levied by the town, Suffolk County and the school districts, yet sets no rate. The Department of Assessment values each parcel, and the elected boards of the school districts, county, town, villages and fire districts decide how much money they need.

The assessor's office compares the levy to a pie: the levy is the whole pie, and your assessment fixes only how large a slice you carry. In most cases the school district tax is the biggest portion of a bill, and it follows the budget residents vote on each May.

When are Smithtown property taxes due?

Smithtown's tax year begins December 1 and ends November 30. One bill is mailed around mid-December, and owners may settle it whole or in two halves. The receiver states that neither date carries a grace period.

How do you pay a Smithtown tax bill?

The Receiver of Taxes works from 99 W. Main Street, with the payment window closing at 4:30 p.m. and summer hours ending earlier, at 4 p.m. The options are:

How does Smithtown assess property, and how do you appeal?

The Department of Assessment sets each property's fair market value. An owner who agrees that the figure matches what a sale would bring needs do nothing, and one who disagrees uses the grievance process. Grievance Day falls on the third Tuesday of May.

Exemptions run on another clock. Applications must reach the department by 5:00 p.m. on March 1, though a STAR application only needs a postmark of that day, and a weekend March 1 pushes the deadline to Monday. An approved exemption shows on the next December bill. Denial letters are mailed by May 1, which leaves time to grieve before Grievance Day.

A cut won through a small claims petition normally appears on the tax bill. If it arrives late in the year, the second half may be adjusted, and if that is too late Suffolk County refunds the owner directly. The assessor's office is at (631) 360-7560. The assessor's list of reasons a bill rises:

  • A new owner who does not qualify for the seller's exemption.

Where is Smithtown, and what communities does it include?

Smithtown occupies the North Shore of Long Island. Long Island Sound lies to its north, Islip to the south, Brookhaven to the east and Huntington to the west. Its 111.5 square miles of total area include 53.8 of land. The Nicolls Patent of 1665, granted to Richard Smith, is taken as the founding date.

Three villages are incorporated within the town: Head of the Harbor, Nissequogue and the Village of the Branch. The hamlets are Smithtown, Kings Park, St. James and Nesconset, along with parts of Commack, Fort Salonga, Hauppauge and Lake Ronkonkoma, several shared with neighboring towns.

Six school districts reach into Smithtown: Smithtown Central, Kings Park Central, Commack, Hauppauge, Sachem and Three Village. The Long Island Rail Road's Port Jefferson Branch stops at Kings Park, Smithtown and St. James. Several of the districts straddle town lines, so read the district name printed on your bill.

Getting around is mostly by car or rail. Suffolk County Transit buses serve the whole town, and the main roads are:

  • NY 25 (Jericho Turnpike and Main Street) and NY 25A, which cross at the Smithtown Bull.
  • NY 111, the main north to south state route, and NY 347, known as the Smithtown Bypass.
  • The Northern State Parkway and the Sunken Meadow State Parkway, with the Long Island Expressway touching only the southwest corner.

Caleb Smith State Park Preserve, Sunken Meadow State Park and Nissequogue River State Park lie within the town, and the town's board meetings are broadcast on its public service television station.

What should you settle before selling a Smithtown house?

Begin with the receiver. Request the amount currently due on your parcel, since neither half has a grace period and unpaid balances after May 31 move to Suffolk County. The tax map number appears on the bill, and the receiver asks for the district, section, block and lot on any mailed check.

Then visit the Building Department at 23 Redwood Lane. It enforces the State building code and the town's zoning, issues permits and certificates of occupancy, and searches its records without charge to see whether each permit has a matching certificate. Work done without a permit will not have one. A home built before permits began in 1947 can request a History Letter. Duplicate certificates with a raised seal are sold for a fee, inspections are booked at (631) 360-7522, and the department does not take applications inside the Village of the Branch, Nissequogue or Head of the Harbor.

Permit triggers the department lists:

  • Pools able to hold water deeper than 24 inches, with a 4 to 6 foot fence or self-latching gate.
  • Fences over four feet tall.
  • Detached sheds over 144 square feet and 12 feet tall, and other accessory structures over 50 square feet.
  • A wider window opening or changed header, and any skylight.
  • New gables or a changed roof pitch, though not simple re-shingling.
  • Decks more than 8 inches above grade.

Deeds are filed with the Suffolk County Clerk in Riverhead. On a $669,900 sale the state's base transfer tax is $2,680, computed on $670,000, and the seller pays it unless the contract says otherwise.

By January 10, without penalty. The bill goes out once a year in mid-December, and the receiver says there is no grace period.

Where do I pay Smithtown taxes after May 31?

To Suffolk County. The Receiver of Taxes cannot take payments postmarked after May 31.

What is the smallest partial payment Smithtown takes?

$200. Penalties apply only to the balance left after the due date.

When is Grievance Day in Smithtown?

The third Tuesday of May. Exemption denials are mailed by May 1, which leaves time to file.

The Department of Assessment must have the application by 5:00 p.m. on March 1, though STAR applications may be postmarked that day. A weekend date moves the deadline to Monday.
